segments.english: Rabbi Akiva says: Laughter and levity accustom a person to lewdness. The Masoretic tradition is a fence for the Torah; tithes are a fence for wealth; vows are a fence for abstinence; a fence for wisdom is silence.
segments.literal: Rabbi Akiva says laughter and-lightness-of head accustom to-lewdness. Tradition fence to-the-Torah. Tithes fence to-wealth. Vows fence to-abstinence. Fence to-wisdom silence.

tokens.note: קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ is an idiom: 'lightness of head', levity, frivolity (the opposite of כֹּבֶד רֹאשׁ, gravity).

Hifil participle plural: two subjects (laughter, levity) take a plural verb; the object ('a person') is left unexpressed in the Hebrew. מַרְגִּילִין comes from רֶגֶל, 'foot': to make someone go habitually, to habituate.
עֶרְוָה, literally 'nakedness'; in rabbinic usage, sexual immorality.

מָסֹרֶת: the Masoretic tradition of the spelling (plene and defective forms) and the reading of the biblical text, as both Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah explain. The pack gives no lexicon key for this word.
סְיָג, 'fence', a protective hedge around something valuable. Vilna spells סייג.
The pack's Jastrow lemma (עָשַׂר) is a verb entry; the noun here is עֹשֶׁר, wealth. Vilna reads לעושר.
פְּרִישׁוּת, 'separation', hence abstinence, self-restraint; a noun from פָּרַשׁ.

phrases.english: Rabbi Akiva says
Laughter and levity
phrases.literal: 'laughter and lightness of head'; the idiom is rendered as one word

phrases.english: accustom a person to lewdness
phrases.literal: 'they habituate to nakedness'; the object 'a person' is supplied by the English

phrases.english: The Masoretic tradition is a fence for the Torah
phrases.literal: 'tradition, a fence to-the-Torah'; the Masorah (spelling and reading) is a protective fence around the written text

phrases.english: tithes are a fence for wealth
phrases.literal: 'tithes, a fence to-wealth'; Bartenura cites עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר, 'tithe in order that you become rich'

phrases.english: vows are a fence for abstinence
a fence for wisdom is silence
phrases.literal: 'a fence to-wisdom, silence'; the word order puts silence last, as the predicate

grammar: The saying is built of four short nominal clauses of the form 'X, a fence for Y', with no verb; the English supplies 'is/are'. The last clause reverses the order (the fence first, then its identity), which puts silence at the end.
מַרְגִּילִין is a Hifil participle, plural masculine, agreeing with the two subjects שְׂחוֹק and קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ.
The tradition (מָסֹרֶת) is listed with tithes, vows and silence: each is a protective fence (סְיָג) around something valuable.
The first sentence is a warning, the next four are the positive fences; the saying is one continuous teaching of Rabbi Akiva.
segments.note: מָסֹרֶת is rendered 'Masoretic tradition' because Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah both say it means the received tradition of plene and defective spellings of the Torah text; the Hebrew word alone could also mean 'tradition' in general. The Jastrow lemma on לָעשֶׁר is a verb entry (עָשַׂר); I keep the data but read the noun 'wealth'. Rambam reads נְדָרִים as a means of acquiring the habit of restraint. For סְיָג לַחָכְמָה שְׁתִיקָה, Bartenura limits the silence to optional talk between people; the English keeps the Hebrew's unlimited wording.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: the tradition the sages handed down about the defective and plene spellings of the Torah is a fence and support for the written Torah, since from it we learn how to perform commandments (for example, the defective and plene spelling of בסכות shows that a sukkah may have three walls).
Bartenura: 'for it is written עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר, tithe in order that you become rich' (Ta'anit 9). Tithing is thus a fence for wealth.
Bartenura: when a person begins abstinence and fears he may transgress, he takes it upon himself in the form of a vow not to do such and such, and by this he subdues his inclination.

Bartenura: the silence is not silence from Torah or from forbidden speech (those are commanded or forbidden anyway) but silence from permitted talk between people, which one should limit as far as possible.

Rambam: when a person vows and keeps his vows, he acquires the habit of abstaining from what he wishes to avoid, and this makes separation easier, meaning guarding against impurities, as in the saying about the garments of the unlearned.

apparatus: Vilna spells מסורת, סייג (four times) and לעושר where the base text reads מָסֹרֶת, סְיָג and לָעשֶׁר; these are spelling variants only.
Bartenura quotes Ta'anit 9a for 'tithe in order that you become rich'; the underlying verse is Deuteronomy 14:22 (עַשֵּׂר תְּעַשֵּׂר).

segments.english: He used to say: Beloved is a human being, for he was created in the image. Extra love was made known to him, that he was created in the image, as it is said (Genesis 9): 'For in the image of God He made the human being.' Beloved are Israel, for they were called children of the Omnipresent. Extra love was made known to them, that they were called children of the Omnipresent, as it is said (Deuteronomy 14): 'You are children of the LORD your God.' Beloved are Israel, for a desirable vessel was given to them. Extra love was made known to them, that a desirable vessel was given to them, by which the world was created, as it is said (Proverbs 4): 'For I have given you good teaching; do not forsake my Torah.'
segments.literal: He was saying: beloved human that-was-created in-image. Love extra is-made-known to-him that-was-created in-image, that-it-was-said (Genesis 9): for in-image-of God He-made [object-marker] the-human. Beloved Israel that-they-were-called children to-the-Place. Love extra is-made-known to-them that-they-were-called children to-the-Place, that-it-was-said (Deuteronomy 14): children you to-YHWH your-God. Beloved Israel that-was-given to-them vessel-of desire. Love extra is-made-known to-them that-was-given to-them vessel-of desire that-in-it was-created the-world, that-it-was-said (Proverbs 4): for teaching good I-have-given to-you my-Torah do-not forsake.

tokens.note: הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: the standard formula 'He used to say': הָיָה with a participle is the habitual past.
חָבִיב is an adjective; the predicate comes first: 'Beloved (is) the human being'.
שֶׁ is a relative particle; here it introduces a reason ('for he was created'), as the sense requires.
בְצֶלֶם has no following word: 'in an image' / 'in the image'. The proof verse supplies 'of God'.
יְתֵרָה: 'extra, surplus': love beyond the first.
Nifal participle of יָדַע: 'is made known' (it was made known to him; Rambam reads that God actually informed him).
The formula שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר introduces a biblical proof text.
אֱלֹהִים is plural in form but singular in meaning: 'God'.
אֵת marks the definite direct object and has no English counterpart.
חֲבִיבִין is plural masculine and the subject יִשְׂרָאֵל is a collective: 'Beloved are Israel'.
הַמָּקוֹם, literally 'the Place', is a name of God: 'the Omnipresent'.
הַמָּקוֹם, literally 'the Place', a name of God: 'the Omnipresent'.
The Tetragrammaton is written לַה' in the text: 'the LORD'.
כְּלִי: 'vessel', 'instrument', here 'a tool'.
חֶמְדָּה: 'desire', 'something desirable'; כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה is a construct chain, 'a precious vessel'.
שֶׁבּוֹ: 'by which', 'through which'; the vessel is the Torah, as Rabbeinu Yonah explains.
לֶקַח: 'teaching', 'instruction' (Bartenura links it to יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי, Deut. 32:2, where the teaching is the Torah).
Qal imperfect 2nd plural with אַל: a prohibition, 'do not forsake'.

phrases.english: He used to say
Beloved is a human being, for he was created in the image
phrases.literal: 'beloved (is) a human being that-was-created in-image'; שֶׁ read as 'for'

phrases.english: Extra love was made known to him
that he was created in the image
phrases.literal: 'that-was-created in-image': what the extra love consists of

phrases.english: as it is said
Genesis 9
For in the image of God He made
the human being
Beloved are Israel, for they were called children of the Omnipresent
phrases.literal: 'beloved Israel that-they-were-called children to-the-Place'; 'the Place' is rendered 'the Omnipresent'

phrases.english: Extra love was made known to them
that they were called children of the Omnipresent
as it is said
Deuteronomy 14
You are children of the LORD your God
Beloved are Israel, for a desirable vessel was given to them
Extra love was made known to them
that a desirable vessel was given to them
by which the world was created
phrases.literal: 'that-in-it was-created the-world'; the vessel is the Torah

phrases.english: as it is said
Proverbs 4
For I have given you good teaching
do not forsake my Torah
phrases.literal: 'my-Torah do-not forsake'; the Hebrew has 'my Torah' before the prohibition

grammar: The saying has three parallel units, each of the same shape: (1) 'Beloved is X, for ...'; (2) 'Extra love was made known to X, that ...'; (3) a proof text introduced by שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר. The repetition is deliberate, and the English keeps it.

חִבָּה יְתֵרָה נוֹדַעַת לוֹ: the verb is a Nifal participle of יָדַע, 'is made known'. The point (Rambam, Bartenura) is that God's telling the human being of the gift is itself a further proof of love.

שֶׁנִּבְרָא, שֶׁנִּקְרְאוּ, שֶׁנִּתַּן are Nifal perfect forms with the relative particle שֶׁ ('that/for'). Three Nifal verbs (was created, were called, was given) carry the argument; the passive leaves God unnamed as the agent until the proof text.
The three proof texts come from Genesis 9:6, Deuteronomy 14:1 and Proverbs 4:2. In the third (Proverbs 4:2) the speaker is God (or wisdom's teacher) addressing Israel about the Torah.
אֱלֹהֵיכֶם is plural construct with a 2nd person plural suffix ('your God'); תּוֹרָתִי is construct with the 1st person singular suffix; the object marker אֶת has no English counterpart.
segments.note: חִבָּה יְתֵרָה: 'extra love' (Jastrow: 'love'; יָתֵר 'surplus'). I keep 'extra' rather than 'special' to preserve the idea of a second, additional love beyond the first. נוֹדַעַת is read 'is made known' (Nifal of יָדַע) following Rambam as quoted by Bartenura: God informs the creature of the gift. The pack's lemma for טוֹב and אָדָם is a proper name in BDB (Tob, Adam); I keep the data and read them as the common adjective and noun. כְּלִי חֶמְדָּה is rendered 'a desirable vessel' to keep the biblical wording of חֶמְדָּה; the vessel is the Torah, by which the world was created. Quotations are translated from the Hebrew of the mishnah, so the verse in Proverbs reads 'my Torah' where the verse itself has תּוֹרָתִי, 'my teaching'.

commentary.summary: Bartenura, citing Rambam: the Holy One showed the human being extra love by informing him that he was created in the image, for one who does a kindness and tells his friend what he has done shows more love than one who does it without telling. Another reading: the extra love is known to him through the verse itself.

Bartenura: everything in the work of creation of which it is said 'and God saw that it was good' was created only for the sake of the Torah, which is called לֶקַח, 'teaching', as in יַעֲרֹף כַּמָּטָר לִקְחִי. The English 'teaching' follows this.

Rambam: letting someone know the measure of the benefit done to him is itself another benefit, for a person sometimes does a kindness out of pity and does not tell the recipient its extent because the recipient seems lowly to him. This is why the Hebrew says extra love is 'made known'.

apparatus: Genesis 9:6 (כִּי בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם).
Deuteronomy 14:1 (בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה' אֱלֹהֵיכֶם).
Proverbs 4:2 (כִּי לֶקַח טוֹב נָתַתִּי לָכֶם תּוֹרָתִי אַל תַּעֲזֹבוּ).
Vilna reads יתירה, שניתן and תעזובו (spelling only), ו for כִּי at 3:14.17, and has extra words א and ב at two places where the base text has none (marked in the pack as variants without a token).

segments.english: Everything is foreseen, yet freedom of choice is given; the world is judged with goodness, and all is according to the abundance of deeds.
segments.literal: The-all foreseen, and-the-permission given, and-in-goodness the-world is-judged, and-the-all according-to-abundance-of the-deed.

tokens.note: הַכֹּל, 'the all', 'everything'.
Qal passive participle of צָפָה, 'to look, see from afar': 'is foreseen' (Rabbeinu Yonah: Psalm 139, 'You know my sitting and rising').
הָרְשׁוּת: literally 'the authority, permission'; here the freedom of choice given to a human being (Rambam: 'the choice is in the hand of every person').
Qal passive participle feminine, agreeing with רְשׁוּת.
וּבְטוֹב: 'and in goodness' (the 'goodness' of God's mercy; Bartenura: the measure of mercy).
Nifal of דָּן: 'is judged'. The pack gives the lemma bdbs:דָּן, which is the proper name Dan; the sense is the verb 'to judge'.
לְפִי: 'according to', literally 'to the mouth of'.
רֹב is ambiguous: 'abundance, greatness' (Bartenura's first reading) or 'majority' (his second reading, the majority of one's deeds). The English keeps 'abundance'.

phrases.english: Everything is foreseen
freedom of choice is given
phrases.literal: 'the-permission given'; רְשׁוּת, 'authority', rendered as freedom of choice following Rambam and Bartenura

phrases.english: the world is judged with goodness
all is according to the abundance of deeds

grammar: Four short clauses, each a noun and a passive participle or verb: הַכֹּל צָפוּי, הָרְשׁוּת נְתוּנָה, הָעוֹלָם נִדּוֹן, הַכֹּל לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. The first two clauses state an apparent tension (foreknowledge and choice) without resolving it.
צָפוּי and נְתוּנָה are passive participles (Qal) used predicatively; the passive leaves the agent, God, unstated.
בְּטוֹב is 'in goodness' (with the preposition בְּ): the world is judged 'with goodness' (by mercy), and the final clause qualifies this: each person receives it in proportion to deeds.
הַכֹּל occurs twice, in the first and the last clause, and carries a different sense each time: 'everything' that happens is foreseen; 'everyone' (or 'all') is judged according to deeds.
segments.note: Rambam's reading of the last clause as 'but not according to the deed' (אֲבָל לֹא עַל פִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה) is a variant; I translate the text of the pack, which reads לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה. הָרְשׁוּת is translated 'freedom of choice' because both normative commentators say it means the power in the hand of a person to do good or evil; the plain sense of the word is 'permission, authority'. For רֹב I keep 'abundance' and give Bartenura's alternative 'majority' in the apparatus.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: everything a person does in the innermost chambers is revealed before Him.
Bartenura: it is in a person's own hand to do good or evil, as it is written (Deut. 30:15) 'See, I have set before you today life...'.

Bartenura: the world is judged with the measure of mercy; and yet not all are equal in this, since everything is according to the abundance of deeds: whoever has many good deeds receives much mercy. He adds another reading: a person is judged by the majority of his deeds (a majority of merits, innocent; of sins, guilty).

Bartenura: according to how much a person repeats and persists in doing good, so his reward is great (a hundred coins given to charity in a hundred separate acts is not like giving them at once). He also records that Rambam's text reads 'but not according to the deed'.

Rambam: the saying includes great matters. 'Everything is foreseen': all that is in the world is known to God. But foreknowledge does not mean compulsion: 'the choice is given', and every person has the choice, as Rambam explained in his eighth chapter. God's judgment of people is by grace and goodness, not strictly by deeds.

apparatus: Bartenura 3:15:4 records Rambam's reading of the last clause: וְהַכֹּל לְפִי רֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, אֲבָל לֹא עַל פִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה ('but not according to the deed').
Bartenura 3:15:3 gives a second reading of רֹב: 'by the majority of his deeds'.
Deuteronomy 30:15 (רְאֵה נָתַתִּי לְפָנֶיךָ הַיּוֹם אֶת הַחַיִּים) is cited by Bartenura for the freedom of choice.
Vilna spells רוב for רֹב.

segments.english: He used to say: Everything is given as a pledge, and a net is spread over all the living. The shop is open, the shopkeeper extends credit, the ledger is open, and the hand writes; and whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow. The collectors make their rounds constantly, every day, and exact payment from a person with his knowledge and without his knowledge. They have what to rely on, and the judgment is a judgment of truth. And everything is prepared for the banquet.
segments.literal: He was saying: the-all given in-pledge, and-net spread over all-of the-living. The-shop open, and-the-shopkeeper extends-credit, and-the-ledger open, and-the-hand writing, and-all the-wishing to-borrow will-come and-will-borrow, and-the-collectors go-around constantly in-every day, and-are-exacted from the-person from-his-knowledge and-that-not from-his-knowledge, and-there-is to-them on what that-they-rely, and-the-judgment judgment-of truth, and-the-all prepared to-the-meal.

tokens.note: Qal passive participle of נָתַן: 'is given'.
בְּעֵרָבוֹן: 'as a pledge', 'in pledge' (a security deposited against a debt).
מְצוּדָה: a net or snare for catching fish or birds (Rabbeinu Yonah: the net of death).
Qal passive participle of פָּרַס, 'to spread out'.
חֶנְוָנִי: shopkeeper, from חֲנוּת 'shop'.
Hifil participle of the root קוף: 'extends credit' (הַקָּפָה, sale on credit).
פִּנְקָס: ledger, record book (Greek loanword).
The hand writes: a participle.
Qal infinitive construct of לָוָה, 'to borrow'. Jastrow has only a cross-reference for this lemma.
Qal imperfect with jussive sense: 'let him come'.
גַּבַּאי: collector (of debts or taxes).
Hifil participle of חָזַר: 'to go around (searching)': the collectors make their rounds.
Nifal participle of פָּרַע: 'is exacted', 'is paid (from)'; the verb takes מִן, 'from (the person)'.
מִדַּעְתּוֹ: 'from his knowledge', i.e. knowingly; Bartenura: sometimes he remembers his debt and says 'You have judged me rightly'.
שֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ: 'without his knowledge'; Bartenura: sometimes he forgets and complains against the judgment of the Omnipresent.
שֶּׁיִּסְמֹכוּ: 'on which they rely' (the collectors rely on the ledger and the shopkeeper's credibility, Bartenura).
אֱמֶת: 'truth'; the construct דִּין אֱמֶת 'a judgment of truth', a just judgment.
Pual participle of תָּקַן: 'is prepared, set in order'.
סְעוּדָה: 'meal, banquet'; Rambam and Bartenura read the world to come.

phrases.english: He used to say
Everything is given as a pledge
a net is spread over all the living
The shop is open
the shopkeeper extends credit
the ledger is open
the hand writes
whoever wishes to borrow may come and borrow
The collectors make their rounds constantly, every day
exact payment from a person with his knowledge and without his knowledge
They have what to rely on
the judgment is a judgment of truth
everything is prepared for the banquet

grammar: The saying is a single extended metaphor: a shop that gives credit. The clauses are strung with 'and' and almost all use participles (נָתוּן, פְּרוּסָה, פְּתוּחָה, מֵקִיף, כּוֹתֶבֶת, מַחֲזִירִים, נִפְרָעִין, מְתֻקָּן), giving the sense of an ongoing, present process.

הַכֹּל נָתוּן בְּעֵרָבוֹן, 'everything is given as a pledge', and the following clause וּמְצוּדָה פְרוּסָה עַל כָּל הַחַיִּים, 'a net is spread over all the living', open the images of security for a debt and of capture.
The pairs מִדַּעְתּוֹ / וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ ('with his knowledge' / 'without his knowledge') contrast the debtor who remembers his debt and the one who has forgotten it.
וְכָל הָרוֹצֶה לִלְווֹת יָבֹא וְיִלְוֶה uses a jussive-like imperfect ('let him come and borrow'): the borrower acts freely, linking to the freedom of choice in the previous mishnah.
The last clause וְהַכֹּל מְתֻקָּן לַסְּעוּדָה resolves the metaphor: the collection ends in a meal. Rambam and Bartenura read the meal as the world to come.
segments.note: The shop metaphor is read as the commentators read it: the shopkeeper is God, the ledger is the record of deeds, the collectors are sufferings and death (Bartenura, Rambam), and the banquet is the world to come. The English keeps the images and puts the application in the commentary, as the saying itself does. מֵקִיף is rendered 'extends credit' (from הַקָּפָה); the pack's lemma is the root קוף. מַחֲזִירִים, 'make their rounds', follows Jastrow's 'to go around (searching)'. The Jastrow entries for בָּא I and לָוָה in the pack give only cross-references or a different meaning, so I give no sense for those verbs; the data are kept. Bartenura's explanations of לְדַעְתּוֹ and שֶׁלֹּא לְדַעְתּוֹ are attached to the whole verse in the pack.

commentary.summary: Bartenura (citing Sukkah 53a): a person's feet are his guarantors; they lead him to the place where he is wanted. Everything is given as a pledge.
Bartenura: the net is suffering and death.
Bartenura: people enter the shop and take goods on credit.
Bartenura: the shopkeeper trusts everyone who comes to take; so people sin every day and the Holy One, blessed be He, waits for them until their time comes.
Bartenura: the ledger is open to write in the credits so that they are not forgotten.
Bartenura: lest one say that the shopkeeper is sometimes busy and does not write everything, the mishnah adds 'and the hand writes'.
Bartenura: this is the same as 'the choice is given' above: no one is forced to borrow against his will.
Bartenura: the collectors are sufferings and bad occurrences.
Bartenura on מִדַּעְתּוֹ: sometimes he remembers his debt and says 'You have judged me well'.
Bartenura on וְשֶׁלֹּא מִדַּעְתּוֹ: sometimes he has forgotten and protests against the judgment of the Omnipresent.

Bartenura: they rely on the ledger and on the shopkeeper, who is believed about his ledger; so the sufferings rely on a person's deeds recorded before the Omnipresent, even though the person has forgotten them.
Bartenura: the Holy One, blessed be He, does not come with a complaint against His creatures (Avodah Zarah 3a); the judgment is just.
Bartenura: righteous and wicked alike have a share in the world to come after the debt has been collected from them.

Rambam: 'the shopkeeper extends credit' means that one's debt may lengthen without being demanded at once; 'whoever wishes to borrow may come' supports the earlier point that there is no compulsion; 'the collectors' is a figure for death and other punishments that come upon a person.
Rambam: the final aim of all this is the life of the world to come.

Rambam: a long note, attached in the pack to the word הָרוֹצֶה in 3:16.21 but about knowledge and understanding (דַּעַת and בִּינָה) of 3:17: each of the two is useful for the existence of the other and completes it. It does not bear on the plain sense of 3:16.

apparatus: Vilna spells ללות for לִלְווֹת, שיסמוכו for שֶּׁיִּסְמֹכוּ and מתוקן for מְתֻקָּן.
Bartenura 3:16:1 cites Sukkah 53a: רַגְלוֹהִי דְּבַר נַשׁ אִינוּן עֲרֵבִין בֵּיהּ (a person's feet are guarantors for him).
Bartenura 3:16:12 cites Avodah Zarah 3a for 'the Holy One does not come with a complaint against His creatures'.
Rambam's note on דעת and בינה (rambam:3:17:1), which concerns 3:17, is anchored in the pack to the word הָרוֹצֶה in 3:16.21.

segments.english: Rabbi Elazar son of Azariah says: If there is no Torah, there is no proper conduct; if there is no proper conduct, there is no Torah. If there is no wisdom, there is no fear; if there is no fear, there is no wisdom. If there is no understanding, there is no knowledge; if there is no knowledge, there is no understanding. If there is no flour, there is no Torah; if there is no Torah, there is no flour. He used to say: Anyone whose wisdom exceeds his deeds, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are many and whose roots are few; and the wind comes and uproots it and overturns it on its face, as it is said (Jeremiah 17): 'He shall be like a bare shrub in the desert plain, and shall not see when good comes; he shall dwell in the parched places of the wilderness, a salt land, uninhabited.' But anyone whose deeds exceed his wisdom, to what is he compared? To a tree whose branches are few and whose roots are many, so that even if all the winds in the world come and blow against it, they do not move it from its place, as it is said (ibid.): 'He shall be like a tree planted by water, and by a stream it sends out its roots, and it shall not see when heat comes; its leaf shall be fresh, and in a year of drought it shall not worry, and it shall not cease from yielding fruit.'
segments.literal: Rabbi Elazar son-of Azariah says: if not Torah, not way-of land; if not way-of land, not Torah. If not wisdom, not fear; if not fear, not wisdom. If not understanding, not knowledge; if not knowledge, not understanding. If not flour, not Torah; if not Torah, not flour. He was saying: all-that his-wisdom is-increased more-than-his-deeds, to-what is-he similar, to-a-tree that-its-branches many and-its-roots few, and-the-wind came and-uproots-it and-overturns-it on its-face, that-it-was-said (Jeremiah 17): and-he-will-be like-a-shrub in-the-desert-plain and-not will-see when will-come good, and-will-dwell parched-places in-the-wilderness land salt and-not will-be-inhabited. But all-that his-deeds are-many more-than-his-wisdom, to-what is-he similar, to-a-tree that-its-branches few and-its-roots many, that-even all-of the-winds that-in-the-world coming and-blowing in-it not move it from-its-place, that-it-was-said (ibid.): and-he-will-be like-a-tree planted on water and-on stream sends-out its-roots and-not will-see when will-come heat, and-will-be its-leaf fresh, and-in-year-of drought not will-worry, and-not will-cease from-doing fruit.

tokens.note: אֵין is the negative existential particle: 'there is not', 'there is no'. The conditional pairs אִם אֵין ... אֵין ... are mirror statements: each term is a condition for the other.

דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ, literally 'the way of the land': proper conduct, decent behavior; it can also mean 'a worldly occupation'. Here the commentators read it as good conduct (Bartenura: dealing well with people; Rabbeinu Yonah: good character traits).
יִרְאָה, 'fear' (of God, or of sin).
בִּינָה, 'understanding'. Bartenura distinguishes it from דַּעַת: בִּינָה derives one thing from another; דַּעַת finds the reason for a thing.
דַּעַת, 'knowledge'.
קֶמַח, 'flour': a metonym for food, livelihood (Bartenura: one who has nothing to eat, how can he occupy himself with Torah?).
הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר: the saying that follows is a second, separate saying of the same sage.
כָּל שֶׁ: 'anyone who', 'whoever'.
Pual participle of רָבָה: 'is increased'.
מִ + מַעֲשָׂיו: comparative מִן, 'more than his deeds'.
לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה: rhetorical question, 'to what is he similar?'
Qal participle of דָּמָה: 'is like'. The pack's lemma bdbs:דָּמָה means 'to cease'; the Hebrew here is the homograph דָּמָה, 'to resemble', and I keep the data.
Pual participle of מָעַט: 'are few'.
וְעוֹקַרְתּוֹ: Qal participle with object suffix, 'and uproots it'.
וְהוֹפַכְתּוֹ: Qal participle with object suffix: 'and overturns it'.
עַרְעָר: a bare or stripped shrub (the meaning is uncertain: juniper, tamarisk, or one stripped, destitute).
עֲרָבָה: desert plain, steppe.
חֲרֵרִים: 'parched places', from חָרֵר, 'to be dry, parched'; the pack gives no lexicon key.
מְלֵחָה: 'salty', a salt land.
Qal imperfect 3rd feminine singular: 'will be inhabited'.
אֲבָל: 'but'; the converse of the first image.
שֶׁאֲפִלּוּ: 'that even'.
Qal participle of נָשַׁב: 'to blow'.
Hifil participle of זָז: 'move, displace'; the pack gives no lexicon key.
אוֹתוֹ: object marker with 3rd person masculine suffix: 'it' (the tree).
Qal passive participle of שָׁתַל: 'planted'.
יוּבַל: 'stream, channel' in Jeremiah 17:8 (the pack lemma is the proper name Jubal, whose etymology is 'stream'; I keep the data).
Piel imperfect of שָׁלַח: 'sends out'.
רַעֲנָן: 'fresh, luxuriant, green'.
בַּצֹּרֶת: 'in drought' (the pack lemma points to a proper name, Zereth; the word means 'drought').
Qal imperfect of דָּאַג: 'worry, be anxious'.
Qal imperfect of מוּשׁ: 'depart, cease'; no lexicon key in the pack.

grammar: The first part is four mirror-image pairs of conditionals אִם אֵין X, אֵין Y / אִם אֵין Y, אֵין X: each of Torah and proper conduct, wisdom and fear, understanding and knowledge, flour and Torah depends on the other. The English keeps the repetition, because the symmetry is the argument.
אֵין is the negative existential particle, not a verb: 'there is not'. In a conditional with אִם: 'if there is no X, there is no Y'.

The second saying is introduced by הוּא הָיָה אוֹמֵר and has two parallel images (tree with many branches and few roots; tree with few branches and many roots), each with the same structure: כָּל שֶׁ... לְמַה הוּא דוֹמֶה, לְאִילָן שֶׁ..., then a proof text. The English keeps the repeated question.
מְרֻבָּה, מְרֻבִּין, מֻעָטִין are Pual participles ('are increased, are decreased'), used as predicate adjectives; the passive implies natural growth.

וְהָרוּחַ בָּאָה וְעוֹקַרְתּוֹ וְהוֹפַכְתּוֹ עַל פָּנָיו: a perfect (בָּאָה) followed by two Qal participles with suffixes; the series describes a quick succession of events. In the second image the verb is the participle: בָּאוֹת וְנוֹשְׁבוֹת, 'coming and blowing'.
Both proof texts are from Jeremiah 17: the first (verse 6) is about 'the one who trusts in man'; the second (verse 8) about 'the one who trusts in the LORD'. The mishnah quotes only the images.
segments.note: דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ: rendered 'proper conduct' because Bartenura and Rabbeinu Yonah both read it as decent behaviour toward people and good character traits in the first pair; in the pair about flour (קֶמַח) the same phrase could be read as 'worldly occupation', and I note that rather than change the word. The mishnah's יִרְאָה is 'fear', without 'of God', as in the Hebrew. For the pair דַּעַת / בִּינָה I follow Bartenura's distinction (דַּעַת 'finds the reason of a thing'; בִּינָה 'derives one thing from another'); the English uses the ordinary words 'knowledge' and 'understanding'. Rabbeinu Yonah describes the two differently (knowledge as what one grasps of oneself, understanding as inferring one thing from another). The pack's lexicon keys for טוֹב, בָּא, דָּמָה, יוּבַל and צֹרֶת point to different words (a place, 'father', 'to cease', a proper name, a proper name); I keep the data, give no sense for them, and read the correct word. Rambam's comment on דעת and בינה is anchored in the pack to 3:16.21 and is ruled on under 3:16.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: if there is no Torah, a person's dealings with people are not good (his conduct is not proper).
Bartenura: if there is no proper conduct, in the end his Torah is forgotten by him.

Bartenura: דַּעַת is finding the reason for a thing; בִּינָה is understanding one thing from another without being shown the reason. Without knowledge to give a reason, there is no understanding; yet understanding comes first, so without understanding there is no knowledge.
Bartenura: one who has nothing to eat, how can he occupy himself with Torah?
Bartenura: what use is the flour in his hand if it has no Torah in it? Better for him that he had no flour and died of hunger.

apparatus: Jeremiah 17:6 (וְהָיָה כְּעַרְעָר בָּעֲרָבָה וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבוֹא טוֹב וְשָׁכַן חֲרֵרִים בַּמִּדְבָּר אֶרֶץ מְלֵחָה וְלֹא תֵשֵׁב).

Jeremiah 17:8 (וְהָיָה כְּעֵץ שָׁתוּל עַל מַיִם וְעַל יוּבַל יְשַׁלַּח שָׁרָשָׁיו וְלֹא יִרְאֶה כִּי יָבֹא חֹם וְהָיָה עָלֵהוּ רַעֲנָן וּבִשְׁנַת בַּצֹּרֶת לֹא יִדְאָג וְלֹא יָמִישׁ מֵעֲשׂוֹת פֶּרִי).
Rabbeinu Yonah (3:17:5, 3:17:6) places knowledge before understanding; Bartenura says understanding comes first (אִם אֵין בִּינָה אֵין דַּעַת).

segments.english: Rabbi Eliezer son of Hisma says: Bird offerings and the openings of the menstruant, these very things are the essentials of the laws. Astronomical cycles and gematria are the desserts of wisdom.
segments.literal: Rabbi Eliezer son-of Hisma says: nests and-openings-of menstruant, they they bodies-of laws. Cycles and-gematriot, desserts to-the-wisdom.

tokens.note: קִנִּין, literally 'nests': the bird offerings (turtledoves and pigeons) of the Temple, from קֵן 'nest' (Bartenura).

פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה: 'openings of the menstruant': the laws of a woman who has lost track of her cycle and must keep watch until she returns to her opening (Bartenura). Rabbeinu Yonah also mentions three places (a house, an upper room, a hall) and the many appearances of blood.
הֵן הֵן: emphatic repetition, 'these very ones' (these, indeed these).
גּוּפֵי: construct plural of גּוּף, 'body, essence': 'the bodies of the laws', hence the essentials, the core.
תְּקוּפוֹת: 'cycles, turnings', i.e. astronomical cycles, the course of the constellations (Bartenura).
גִּימַטְרִיָּה: gematria, the counting of the numerical values of letters (a Greek loanword).
פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת: 'dessert', the sweets eaten at the end of a meal (Bartenura; Greek loanword).
The preposition ל here means 'for, of': 'the desserts (belonging) to wisdom'.

grammar: Two sentences, each of two coordinated nouns followed by a predicate. The first has a doubled pronoun, הֵן הֵן, which marks emphasis: 'these, only these'. The second has no pronoun at all; the predicate is the single noun פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת.
קִנִּין is the plural of קֵן ('nest') used as a technical term for bird offerings. פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה is a construct chain, 'openings of the menstruant'.
גּוּפֵי הֲלָכוֹת is a construct chain: 'bodies of laws', meaning the core or essentials.

תְּקוּפוֹת, גִּימַטְרִיאוֹת and פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת are loan words (Greek in origin) that the mishnah uses as technical terms. The contrast of גּוּף ('body') with פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת ('after-dishes') is the point of the saying: the essential versus the ornamental.
segments.note: Two choices to record. פִּתְחֵי נִדָּה: the English keeps the literal 'the openings of the menstruant' because the sense of 'openings' is not simple (Bartenura: her opening or onset; Rabbeinu Yonah: three places in the house, and many appearances of blood). קִנִּין is rendered 'bird offerings' following Bartenura, with the literal 'nests' in the gloss. פַּרְפְּרָאוֹת is 'desserts' following Bartenura's image of the sweets eaten at the end of a meal, which continues the meal metaphor of the previous mishnah. The Jastrow entry for גּוּף I in the pack does not match the noun 'body' here, so I give no sense for it; the data are kept.

commentary.summary: Bartenura: the bird offerings are called קִנִּין, from 'a bird's nest' (קַן צִפּוֹר); they contain weighty laws, for example when an obligatory offering is mixed with a freewill one, or a burnt offering (whose rites are above) with a sin offering (whose rites are below).

Bartenura: the laws of a menstruant woman who has lost her regular time and must keep watch until she returns to her 'opening'; sometimes she must immerse ninety-five times, according to the view that immersion at its proper time is a commandment.
Bartenura: these are the core of the Oral Torah, for which one receives reward.
Bartenura: תְּקוּפוֹת concerns the course of the constellations.
Bartenura: גִּימַטְרִיאוֹת is the counting of letters.
Bartenura: as the dessert eaten at the end of a meal for the sake of cleansing the palate and enjoyment, so these branches of wisdom bring honor to those who know them in the eyes of people.

apparatus: Vilna spells קינין for קִנִּין and וגמטריאות for וְגִימַטְרִיאוֹת.

Rabbeinu Yonah (3:18:1) gives the name as רבי אלעזר חסמא (Rabbi Elazar Hisma), against the base text רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר בֶּן חִסְמָא, and glosses קִנִּים as the nests of doves of women who have given birth.
Rabbeinu Yonah (3:18:3) cites Bava Metzia 84b: sixty colors of blood were brought before him and he ruled all of them pure blood.
